newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Religious police tighten up in Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Religious police tighten up in Kabul.

text.p: The Taleban's religious police have tightened regulations in Kabul, punishing 700 travellers for trimming their beards and beating at least two female doctors, according to Taleban radio and international aid workers in Kabul.

"Seven hundred passengers who were travelling on the Kabul to Kandahar (in southern Afghanistan) highway were punished in accordance with Islamic law for trimming or cutting their beards," said a broadcast on Taleban-controlled Radio Shariat on Tuesday night.
The department was acting on the orders of the acting Minister of Justice, Mullah Nuruddin Turabi, according to the report.

The Taleban's religious police, formally known as the Ama bin Marouf wa Nahi al Munkar (Department for Prevention of Vice and Promotion of Virtue), has decreed that men should not shave or trim their beards. A beard must be long enough to protrude from a fist clenched at the base of the chin, the decree says.
The Radio Shariat report did not say how the beard-trimmers were punished.

There has also been at least one incident involving religious police beating at least two female doctors and possibly other female medical staff at the hospital where they worked, according to aid workers in Kabul.

No one directly involved in the incident was willing to comment. But an aid worker said that it followed a series of decrees from the religious police that will increase the difficulties faced by international aid workers trying to deliver medical and other relief aid to Kabul's hard-pressed population.
When the Taleban first arrived in Kabul last September, they banned women from working outside the home, except in the medical sector.

But even medical workers are subject to restrictions on what they can wear and whom they can see. On July 16 the religious police issued a decree restating those restrictions and introducing further limitations.

"Women are not allowed to work in any field except the medical sector. Aid agencies need to gain permission from the Department for Promoting Virtue and Preventing Vice to employ or assist women," says the July 16 decree, which was distributed to aid agencies and hospitals in Kabul.
But the decree says women are not allowed to hold positions of authority in hospitals.
"No Afghan woman can take a senior or acting senior position in foreign-run hospitals," it says.

Further items in the decree banned women from wearing jewellery and make-up, from making a noise with their shoes when they walked, and from sitting beside the driver when travelling to and from work.

"Stylish dress and decoration of women in hospitals is forbidden. Women are duty bound to behave with dignity, to walk calmly and refrain from hitting their shoes on the ground, which makes noises," said the decree.
"Women working in the medical sector should not sit next to the driver during transportation. No Afghan woman has the right to be transported in the same car as foreigners."
Shortly after they were issued, an aid worker called the regulations impractical and said that they effectively shut down aid programmes.

"They are impractical. If we implemented according to the regulations, we would have to stop all our programmes," said Ross Everson of the aid umbrella organisation Agency Coordinating Body for Afghan relief.
The religious police are a semi-autonomous department reporting directly to Mullah Mohammed Omar, the leader of the Taleban movement.
